Abstract
Background  As non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) becomes increasingly common and affects population 
health, simple and effective screening tools for NAFLD are essential. The triglyceride high-density cholesterol-glucose 
body index (TyHGB), a novel metabolic index, has shown promise for predicting metabolic disorders. The objective of 
this research was to assess TyHGB’s predictive capability for NAFLD across two distinct cohorts.
Methods  This retrospective study utilized data obtained from two independent cohorts: a Chinese hospital cohort 
(n = 181,241) and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cohort (n = 3,286). TyHGB was 
computed according to the following equation: triglyceride level/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol level + 0.7 × 
fasting blood glucose level (mmol/L) + 0.1 × body mass index (kg/m²). NAFLD was diagnosed using ultrasonography. 
The TyHGB-NAFLD association was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression analysis, restricted cubic spline 
methodology, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. To establish the added predictive capacity of 
TyHGB over the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination 
improvement (IDI) were determined.
Results  In both cohorts, participants with higher TyHGB values demonstrated a significantly higher prevalence 
of NAFLD. After full adjustment for potential confounders, the odds ratios for NAFLD on comparing the highest 
versus lowest quartiles of TyHGB were 12.22 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.73–13.93) in the Chinese cohort 
and 3.17 (95% CI: 2.25–4.46) in the NHANES cohort. Restricted cubic spline modeling demonstrated significant 
nonlinear associations between TyHGB values and NAFLD risk in both populations (P for nonlinearity < 0.001). TyHGB 
demonstrated superior discriminative ability for NAFLD in comparison with the TyG index, with area under the curve 
(AUC) values of 0.8410 versus 0.7995 in the Chinese cohort and 0.6492 versus 0.5952 in the NHANES cohort (both 
P < 0.001). Adding TyHGB to the baseline prediction models significantly improved risk discrimination, with greater 
improvements than those achieved by adding TyG (NRI: 0.0183, 95% CI: 0.015–0.0217; IDI: 0.0067, 95% CI: 0.0057–
0.0076; both P < 0.001).

Introduction
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) has emerged 
as one of the most prevalent chronic Liver diseases 
worldwide, with a recent systematic review reporting 
a global prevalence of 30.05% (95% confidence interval 
[CI]: 27.88%−32.32%), and with an alarming increase of 
50.4% from 25.26% in 1990–2006 to 38.00% in 2016–
2019 [1]. Now termed metabolic dysfunction-associated 
steatotic liver disease (MASLD), this disorder represents 
a continuum ranging from simple steatosis to metabolic 
dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, affecting approxi­
mately 3%−5% of patients progressing to cirrhosis over 
20 years and showing a subsequent risk of hepatocellular 
carcinoma [2, 3]. NAFLD’s global health burden progres­
sively increases in conjunction with the expanding preva­
lence of obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and metabolic 
syndrome [4, 5]. However, NAFLD can manifest in non-
obese persons, notably in Asian demographic groups, 
with occurrence rates of 10%−20% observed among indi­
viduals maintaining normal body mass index (BMI) lev­
els, highlighting the heterogeneous pathomechanisms, 
including dysfunctional adipose tissue, dysregulated hep­
atokine secretion, and organ crosstalk, that contribute to 
disease development beyond simple adiposity [6, 7]. The 
substantial public health burden of NAFLD has necessi­
tated the development of accessible and reliable screen­
ing tools to identify at-risk individuals early and enable 
timely interventions.
While insulin resistance (IR) is commonly considered 
a central driver of NAFLD pathogenesis, recent evi­
dence has highlighted the substantial heterogeneity in 
the disease pathophysiology, with some patients devel­
oping hepatic steatosis through IR-independent mecha­
nisms, including dysfunctional adipose tissue, subclinical 
inflammation, and dysregulated hepatokine secretion 
[7–9]. The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, calculated 
as ln(fasting triglyceride [mg/dL] × fasting plasma glu­
cose [mg/dL]/2), has been proposed as a simple, reliable, 
and cost-effective surrogate marker for IR, and has been 
associated with NAFLD risk across diverse populations 
[10–12]. Previous studies have established a negative 
correlation between high-density lipoprotein cholesterol 
(HDL-C) concentrations and NAFLD, while showing 
positive correlations between NAFLD and triglyceride 
(TG), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and 
total cholesterol (TC) levels [13, 14]. However, the TyG 
index primarily reflects glucose and triglyceride dynam­
ics, potentially overlooking other critical components 
such as the HDL-C level and body composition, which 
have also been implicated in NAFLD development [15]. 
Although TyG has shown utility in NAFLD prediction, 
it has several notable limitations: (1) it does not account 
for HDL-C, which plays a protective role against hepatic 
steatosis through its involvement in reverse cholesterol 
transport and its anti-inflammatory properties [16]; (2) it 
fails to incorporate body composition metrics, which are 
established independent risk factors for NAFLD; and (3) 
it could fail to comprehensively reflect the multifaceted 
relationships between diverse metabolic parameters that 
collectively contribute to NAFLD pathogenesis.
The triglyceride high-density cholesterol-glucose body 
index (TyHGB), a novel modification of the TyG index 
that incorporates the HDL-C level and BMI, was recently 
developed to enhance the predictive capability for IR-
related conditions [17, 18]. This index is calculated using 
the following formula: TG/HDL-C + 0.7 × fasting plasma 
glucose (mmol/L) + 0.1 × BMI (kg/m²); the TyHGB was 
initially validated for predicting IR in patients with ges­
tational diabetes mellitus (GDM) [17, 18]. TyHGB offers 
several potential advantages over the conventional TyG 
index: (1) it integrates the TG/HDL-C ratio, which has 
been demonstrated to be more strongly associated with 
IR and hepatic steatosis than either parameter alone [9]; 
(2) it directly incorporates BMI to address the critical role 
of adiposity in NAFLD pathophysiology; and (3) it offers 
a more thorough evaluation of metabolic dysfunction by 
capturing multiple parameters in a single metric. By inte­
grating the HDL-C level and BMI with TG and fasting 
glucose levels, TyHGB can capture a more comprehen­
sive metabolic profile. Additionally, TyHGB components 
are routinely measured in clinical practice, making them 
practical tools that require no additional testing beyond 
standard laboratory assessments. Given the shared met­
abolic underpinnings of NAFLD and GDM, namely, IR, 
dyslipidemia, and adiposity, TyHGB holds promise as 
a novel tool for NAFLD risk assessment. However, to 
date, no investigations have examined the performance 
of TyHGB in predicting NAFLD, nor have its predictive 
capabilities been compared to the established TyG index 
across different populations.

The study hypothesis proposed that TyHGB, by incor­
porating the HDL-C level and BMI alongside the estab­

predictive performance for NAFLD in comparison with 
the TyG index alone. Specifically, this study sought to (1) 
determine whether TyHGB offers incremental value over 
the established TyG index for identifying NAFLD risk, (2) 
evaluate the consistency of TyHGB’s performance across 
ethnically diverse populations, and (3) quantify the 
potential clinical utility of TyHGB as a practical screen­
ing tool for NAFLD in routine clinical practice.
Methods
Study design and participants
This retrospective investigation utilized information 
from an extensive hospital-based health screening data­
base developed by the Wenzhou Medical Center at Wen­
zhou People’s Hospital in China. To reduce selection bias, 
participant data from health examinations were gathered 
sequentially and without selection criteria from January 
2010 to December 2014. This dataset has been previ­
ously described and employed in multiple publications 
investigating associations between various metabolic 
markers and NAFLD [19–21]. For the present analysis, 
we initially enrolled 181,241 adult participants who had 
undergone comprehensive health examinations including 
liver ultrasonography (Fig. 1). Participants were excluded 
on the basis of the following criteria: (1) substantial alco­
hol consumption (> 140 g/week for male and > 70 g/week 
for female); (2) presence of other chronic liver diseases, 
including viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, or 
autoimmune hepatitis; (3) use of medications known 
to influence hepatic steatosis or metabolic parameters 
(including antihypertensive agents, antidiabetic agents, 
or lipid-lowering medications); (4) incomplete data nec­
essary for calculation of TyHGB and the TyG index; 
and (5) missing liver ultrasonography results. The raw 
data were obtained from the DATADRYAD database 
(https://datadryad.org/stash) under DOI:​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​d​o​i​.​o​r​g​/​

Committee, and informed consent was acquired from all 
study participants. For this secondary analysis, individual 
identifiers were deleted, and health examination num­
bers were used instead of personal information to ensure 
confidentiality.
The findings were validated in a varied population 
through analysis of NHANES data from the 2017–2018 
cycle. From the initial NHANES 2017–2018 popula­
tion, 3,286 adult participants with complete data for liver 
ultrasonography findings, TG, HDL-C, and fasting blood 
glucose (FBG) levels, and BMI required for the calcula­
tion of TyHGB were included (Fig. 1). Exclusion criteria 
similar to those used in the Chinese cohort were applied. 
Individuals with heavy alcohol intake, viral hepatitis, or 
other established liver pathologies were eliminated, as 
were those taking medications that may affect hepatic 
steatosis or metabolism. Patients with BMI > 25  kg/m2 
were not excluded from the NHANES cohort, which 
served as a validation population with more diverse body 
composition profiles and allowed us to assess the gener­
alizability of TyHGB across different body habitus rep­
resentations. Thus, we could directly test whether the 
superior performance of TyHGB over TyG would persist 
in participants with a higher BMI (including obese par­
ticipants), in participants with elevated LDL-C levels, 
and in a more metabolically diverse population. This 
approach strengthens our findings, since TyHGB main­
tained its superiority despite the increased heterogeneity.

Ultrasonographic diagnosis of NAFLD
In the Chinese hospital cohort, NAFLD diagnosis was 
established through ultrasonographic evaluation fol­
lowing guidelines from the Chinese Liver Disease 
Association [22]. Qualified technicians without access 
to participants’ clinical and laboratory information 
conducted the ultrasound evaluations. NAFLD was 
characterized by diffuse intensification of near-field echo­
genicity in the liver (exceeding that of kidney and spleen) 
with progressive far-field echo attenuation when accom­
panied by any of these characteristics: (1) indistinct 
intrahepatic vascular structure visualization, (2) mild-to-
moderate liver enlargement with rounded, blunt margins, 
(3) diminished blood flow signals with preserved normal 
flow patterns, and (4) poor or incomplete delineation of 
the right hepatic lobe boundary and diaphragmatic inter­
face. NAFLD was diagnosed when at least two experi­
enced ultrasonographers agreed on the findings. When 
discordant findings occurred, a third senior ultrasonog­
rapher was engaged to establish consensus.
For the NHANES cohort, transient elastography via 
FibroScan model 502 V2 Touch was employed for hepatic 
steatosis assessment. The FibroScan device utilizes 
vibration-controlled transient elastography to generate 
liver stiffness measurements while concurrently assess­
ing ultrasound attenuation associated with liver steato­
sis through the controlled attenuation parameter (CAP). 
In accordance with established diagnostic thresholds, 
NAFLD was defined as a CAP score ≥ 248 dB/m in the 
absence of significant alcohol consumption (defined as 
> 3 drinks/day in male and > 2 drinks/day in female) and 
other known causes of liver disease, including viral hepa­
titis (hepatitis B virus [HBV] or hepatitis C virus [HCV] 
infections) [23–25]. Participants with HBV or HCV 
infection were identified on the basis of positive serologi­
cal test results or self-reported diagnoses.
Covariates
In the Chinese hospital cohort, comprehensive data for 
clinical and biochemical parameters were collected dur­
ing health examinations. Blood specimens were obtained 
following a minimum 8-hour overnight fasting period 
and analyzed in a hospital laboratory using standardized 
methods. The demographic information included data 
for age and sex. Anthropometric assessments encom­
passed weight and height measurements, obtained while 
participants wore minimal clothing without footwear. 
BMI was computed as body weight in kilograms divided 
by height squared in meters (kg/m²). Blood pressure was 
recorded in a seated position after a 5-min rest using an 
automated sphygmomanometer. Laboratory assessments 
included liver function tests for measurement of alanine 
aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase 
(AST), gamma glutamyl transferase (GGT), total protein, 
albumin, globulin, total bilirubin, and direct bilirubin 
levels. Kidney function was evaluated on the basis of the 
blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and uric acid levels. Lipid 
parameter evaluation included TC, TG, HDL-C, and 
LDL-C determinations. FBG levels were also measured. 
All biochemical analyses were conducted using an auto­
mated analyzer (Abbott AxSYM) and standard methods.
For the NHANES cohort, a comprehensive set of 
demographic, socioeconomic, and clinical variables was 
collected using standardized protocols, including ques­
tionnaires, physical evaluations, and laboratory mea­
surements. Demographic information included data for 
age, sex (male, female), and race/ethnicity (categorized 
as Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, Mexican 
American, and Others). Socioeconomic factors, such 
as education achievement (categorized as below high 
school, high school, and above high school), marital sta­
tus (categorized as unmarried or married), and household 
income were also recorded. Anthropometric measure­
ments included measurement of waist circumference 
and BMI. Clinical variables encompassed cardiovascu­
lar disease (CVD), characterized as participant-reported 
diagnoses of heart failure, coronary heart disease, angina, 
myocardial infarction, or stroke. Diabetes was defined 
as having been diagnosed by a doctor or having a fast­
ing blood sugar level of ≥ 126 mg/dL. Hypertension was 
defined as blood pressure readings of 140/90 mmHg or 
above or a prior diagnosis of hypertension in participants 
not currently taking antihypertensive medications (since 
those on antihypertensive therapy were excluded from 
the analysis). Smoking patterns were grouped as never 
smoker, former smoker, or current smoker. Blood pres­
sure assessment was conducted following a 5-minute 
rest period with individuals in a seated posture, and the 
mean of three measurements was utilized for analysis. 
Blood specimens were obtained following overnight fast­
ing and analyzed at the NHANES Health and Nutrition 
Examination Center. Laboratory measurements included 
measurement of liver enzyme (ALT and AST), lipid pro­
file (TC, HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides), FBG, and 
glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels. Prescription medi­
cation usage, including blood pressure, diabetes, and 
cholesterol medications, was documented through self-
reports and medication inventories. Study participants 
were eliminated if they demonstrated considerable alco­
hol consumption, viral hepatitis, additional confirmed 
liver disorders, or pharmaceutical therapy that could

The TyHGB index was derived through the following cal­

m²), while the comparison marker TyG index was com­

Statistical analysis
Normally 
distributed 
continuous 
variables 
were 
described using mean ± standard deviation, while non-
normally distributed data were expressed as medians 
with interquartile ranges [Q1, Q3]. Categorical data were 
displayed as frequency (percentage). Baseline charac­
teristic variations among TyHGB quartiles were evalu­
ated using the Kruskal–Wallis test for non-normally 
distributed data and one-way ANOVA for normally 
distributed data, while categorical variables were ana­
lyzed using chi-square tests. Missing data were handled 
through k-nearest neighbor (KNN) imputation to maxi­
mize the utilization of available data. Prior to perform­
ing the primary analyses, multicollinearity evaluation 
among covariates was conducted using the variance infla­
tion factor (VIF) methodology. Covariates with VIF val­
ues exceeding 5 were deemed to demonstrate substantial 
collinearity and underwent careful assessment for final 
model inclusion.
The TyHGB index was analyzed both as a categorical 
variable (by quartiles) and as a continuous variable. To 
examine the association between TyHGB and NAFLD, 
multivariable logistic regression models were utilized, 
and odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (95% 
CIs) were calculated. Three stepwise adjustment mod­
els were established: Model I (unadjusted); Model II 
(adjusted for sex, age, and BMI for the Chinese cohort; 
sex, age, BMI, and race/ethnicity for the NHANES 
cohort); and Model III (for the Chinese cohort: fully 
adjusted for sex, age, BMI, and GGT, ALT, TC, AST, 
LDL-C, total protein, total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, 
blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and uric acid; for the 
NHANES cohort: fully adjusted for sex, age, BMI, race/
ethnicity, marital status, blood urea nitrogen, CVD, 
smoking status, AST, diabetes, albumin, hypertension, 
creatinine, ALT, uric acid, TC, and LDL-C levels). Lin­
ear trends were performed by incorporating the median 
value of each TyHGB quartile as a continuous variable 
within the regression analyses.
For investigating possible nonlinear associations 
between TyHGB and NAFLD risk, restricted cubic spline 
(RCS) modeling was conducted with knots placed at the 
5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles of the TyHGB dis­
tribution. The significance of nonlinear relationships 
was evaluated using likelihood ratio tests that com­
pared linear-term models against spline-term models. 
The predictive performance of TyHGB for NAFLD was 
evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) 
curve analysis, with the area under the ROC curve (AUC) 
calculated with the 95% CIs. DeLong’s test was used to 
compare the AUCs of the TyHGB and TyG index. Net 
reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated dis­
crimination improvement (IDI) calculations were con­
ducted without category constraints to quantify the 
incremental value of incorporating TyHGB or TyG into 
baseline risk assessment models.
The baseline prediction model for the Chinese cohort 
included sex, age, total protein, BMI, total bilirubin, GGT, 
blood urea nitrogen, ALT, direct bilirubin, AST, creati­
nine, TC, uric acid, and LDL-C levels. For the NHANES 
cohort, the baseline model included sex, age, BMI, race/
ethnicity, marital status, CVD, smoking status, diabetes, 
hypertension, and ALT, AST, albumin, creatinine, uric 
acid, blood urea nitrogen, TC, and LDL-C levels. Data 
analysis was were performed using R software (version 
4.1.0; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, 
Austria) and EmpowerStats software (​h​t​t​p​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​e​m​p​
o​w​e​r​s​t​a​t​.​o​r​g​/​e​n​/). Statistical significance was defined as 
P < 0.05 across all analyses.
Results
Baseline demographic and clinical features across TyHGB 
quartiles
Participant baseline demographic and clinical charac­
teristics from Chinese and NHANES populations, cat­
egorized according to TyHGB quartiles, are shown in 
Tables 1 and 2, respectively. Significant variations among 
TyHGB quartiles were identified in both populations for 
most demographic, anthropometric, and biochemical 
characteristics (all P < 0.001).
In the Chinese cohort, age and sex distributions differed 
significantly across the TyHGB quartiles. Participants 
in the higher TyHGB quartiles were significantly older 
and included a significantly higher proportion of males, 
with male representation rising from 20.65% in Q1 to 
77.83% in Q4 (P < 0.001). BMI increased significantly with 
increasing TyHGB quartiles (P < 0.001). Liver enzyme 
levels differed significantly across the TyHGB quartiles. 
The mean GGT level increased from 17.97 ± 11.07 IU/L 
in Q1 to 41.29 ± 41.56 IU/L in Q4, and the ALT level 
increased from 15.34 ± 14.25 IU/L to 25.28 ± 17.99 IU/L 
(both P < 0.001). Consistent patterns were identified for 
Lipid parameters, with the TC and LDL-C levels increas­
ing from 4.37 ± 0.71 to 4.72 ± 0.73 mmol/L and 2.06 ± 0.45 
to 2.40 ± 0.45 µmol/L, respectively (both P < 0.001). Cre­
atinine and uric acid levels also increased significantly 
across TyHGB quartiles (P < 0.001).
The NHANES cohort exhibited comparable patterns, 
with older and predominantly male participants in the 
higher TyHGB quartiles (P < 0.001). Notably, the increase

Diabetes prevalence showed a substantial increase from

whereas the prevalence of hypertension increased from 
12.41% to 30.86% (both P < 0.001). Similarly, CVD was 
more prevalent in higher TyHGB quartiles (2.07% in Q1 
vs. 4.25% in Q4; P = 0.014).
Nonlinear relationship between TyHGB and the risk of 
NAFLD
RCS analyses were performed to exam the dose-response 
association between TyHGB and NAFLD risk in both 
cohorts (Fig.  2). In the Chinese cohort, a notable non­
linear association was confirmed between TyHGB 
and NAFLD (P for nonlinearity, < 0.001; Fig.  2A). This 
relationship exhibited a J-shaped curve with minimal 
risk at lower TyHGB values, followed by a progres­
sive increase in NAFLD risk as TyHGB values increased 
beyond a certain threshold. Specifically, the risk remained 
relatively flat at lower TyHGB values, but increased expo­
nentially thereafter, with the steepest gradient observed 
at higher values. At the highest observed TyHGB values, 
the adjusted odds ratio for NAFLD exceeded 10.0, dem­
onstrating the substantial discriminative capacity of this 
index. The NHANES cohort also showed a similar sig­
nificant nonlinear relationship (P for nonlinearity < 0.001; 
Fig.  2B), but with a different pattern. The association 
in the NHANES cohort demonstrated an initial sharp 
increase in the NAFLD risk at lower TyHGB values, fol­
lowed by a more gradual positive slope at higher values.

Additive predictive capacity of the TyHGB index for NAFLD
The discriminative performance of TyHGB for NAFLD 
was evaluated using the ROC curve analysis (Fig. 3). In 
the Chinese cohort, TyHGB demonstrated superior pre­
dictive ability in comparison with the TyG index, with 
an AUC of 0.8410 (95% CI: 0.8385–0.8434) versus 0.7995 
(95% CI: 0.7981–0.8050) for TyG (P < 0.001 by DeLong’s 
test, Fig. 3A). Similarly, in the NHANES cohort, TyHGB 
exhibited significantly better discriminative capacity for 
NAFLD, with an AUC of 0.6492 (95% CI: 0.6302–0.6681) 
in comparison with the TyG index, which had an AUC of 
0.5952 (95% CI: 0.5737–0.6145) (P < 0.001, Fig. 3B). These 
findings indicate that TyHGB consistently outperformed 
TyG in identifying NAFLD across both populations, 
despite the overall lower AUC values in the NHANES 
cohort.
To further assess the potential clinical utility of these 
indices, their incremental value when added to estab­
lished risk prediction models was examined (Fig. 4). In 
the Chinese cohort, the baseline model incorporating 
conventional risk factors yielded an AUC of 0.8173 (95% 
CI: 0.8144–0.8201). Adding the TyG index to this base­
line model significantly improved the AUC to 0.8518 
(95% CI: 0.8494–0.8545) (P < 0.001), while incorporating 
TyHGB further enhanced the predictive performance 
to an AUC of 0.8616 (95% CI: 0.8591–0.8640) (P < 0.001 
in comparison with the baseline model and the baseline 
model plus TyG, Fig.  4A). Similarly, in the NHANES 
cohort, the addition of TyHGB to the baseline model 
(AUC: 0.7127, 95% CI: 0.6939–0.7319) resulted in a 
greater improvement in predictive performance (AUC: 
0.7280, 95% CI: 0.7095–0.7466) in comparison with the 
addition of TyG (AUC: 0.7241, 95% CI: 0.7057–0.7443), 
with significant differences between all model compari­
sons (all P < 0.05, Fig. 4B).
The incremental value of TyHGB over both the base­
line model and the baseline model plus TyG was further 
quantified using the NRI and IDI (Fig. 5). In the Chinese 
cohort, adding TyHGB to the baseline model yielded a 
significant NRI of 0.082 (95% CI: 0.0772–0.0868) and an 
IDI of 0.077 (95% CI: 0.0749–0.0792) (both P < 0.001), 
which were greater than the improvements observed with 
TyG (NRI: 0.0631, 95% CI: 0.0578–0.0684; IDI: 0.0704, 
95% CI: 0.0685–0.0722; both P < 0.001). Notably, replac­

0.015–0.0217) and IDI (0.0067, 95% CI: 0.0057–0.0076) 
(both P < 0.001), demonstrating the incremental value 
of TyHGB beyond TyG. The NHANES cohort exhibited

Sensitivity analysis
To evaluate the influence of different exclusion criteria 
on our findings, a sensitivity analysis was conducted by 
applying the same BMI and LDL-C restrictions to the 
NHANES cohort. Among the 771 participants meet­
ing these criteria, adding TyHGB to the baseline model 
improved the AUC from 0.7056 (95% CI: 0.6429–0.7660) 
to 0.7326 (95% CI: 0.6720–0.7891), showing a trend 
toward significance (P = 0.062). This improvement was 
more pronounced than that achieved by adding TyG, 
which increased the AUC to 0.7306 (95% CI: 0.6722–
0.7836, P = 0.172 vs. baseline; Supplementary Fig.  1). 
Notably, the incremental value of TyHGB over the 
baseline model was substantial: the NRI of 0.3168 (95% 
CI: 0.1723–0.4612, P < 0.001) and IDI of 0.0245 (95% 
CI: 0.0066–0.0424, P = 0.00732) indicated significant 
improvements in risk classification and discrimination. 
When comparing TyHGB to TyG, statistical significance 
was not achieved (P = 0.415), likely due to the reduced 
sample size, the NRI (0.0276, 95% CI: −0.0681-0.1234) 
and IDI (0.0021, 95% CI: −0.0017-0.0058) showed consis­
tent trends favoring TyHGB (Supplementary Fig. 2).
Discussion
This study presented a comprehensive evaluation of 
TyHGB as a novel predictor of NAFLD in two inde­
pendent populations. The findings convincingly dem­
onstrated that TyHGB exhibits superior predictive 
performance in comparison with the established TyG 
index in both the Chinese hospital and NHANES 
cohorts. A robust, dose-dependent relationship between 
TyHGB and NAFLD risk was consistently observed 
across both populations, with the highest TyHGB quar­
tile being associated with substantially increased odds of 
NAFLD in comparison with the lowest quartile in both 
cohorts. TyHGB demonstrated superior discriminative 
performance for NAFLD compared to TyG, as evidenced 
by higher AUC values in both cohorts. Furthermore, add­
ing TyHGB to the baseline prediction models yielded 
significant improvements in risk reclassification and dis­
crimination metrics (NRI and IDI), with greater improve­
ments than those achieved by adding TyG. These findings 
collectively suggest that TyHGB represents an advance­
ment over the existing metabolic indices for NAFLD risk 
assessment.
The TyHGB index is an extension of the established 
TyG index that incorporates additional metabolic param­
eters, namely the HDL-C level and BMI, to improve its 
utility as a comprehensive assessment tool. The TyG 
index has proven to be a beneficial marker for metabolic 
dysfunction evaluation without the need for direct insulin 
measurement, thus providing a cost-effective approach 
for evaluating IR across various clinical environments

The present findings indicate that TyHGB demonstrates 
robust and superior performance in predicting NAFLD 
in comparison with the established TyG index across 
diverse populations. These results are consistent with and 
expand upon existing research on metabolic indices and 
NAFLD prediction. Previous research have established 
the value of the TyG index as a cost-effective and easily 
accessible alternative for NAFLD risk assessment [33]. 
The TyG index acts as a substitute biomarker for IR, a 
critical component in the development of NAFLD, and its 
predictive capability has been confirmed across various 
ethnicities [10, 34]. Studies have also explored the combi­
nation of TyG with other anthropometric measurements 
to improve the prediction of NAFLD. Notably, the TyG-
BMI index provides superior predictive performance 
for NAFLD compared to TyG used independently [33]. 
In a study of non-obese patients, TyG-BMI exhibited 
enhanced performance relative to TyG alone in evaluat­
ing NAFLD risk [35]. Furthermore, TyG-BMI exhibited 
the highest AUC for predicting NAFLD in patients with 
type 2 diabetes [36]. Similarly, TyG-related parameters 
such as TyG-WC (waist circumference) and TyG-WHtR 
(waist-to-height ratio) have shown greater predictive 
capacity for NAFLD than the TyG index alone [33, 37]. 
The present findings extend this line of research by incor­
porating the HDL-C level and BMI with the TyG index to 
yield a single comprehensive metric. The consistent supe­
riority of TyHGB over TyG in both cohorts suggests that 
the incorporation of additional metabolic parameters 
better captures the multifaceted metabolic determinants 
of NAFLD. This aligns with the expanding understanding 
that NAFLD represents more than just a hepatic com­
ponent of metabolic syndrome but a complex condition 
influenced by interrelated metabolic pathways involving 
lipid metabolism, glucose homeostasis, and adiposity 
[38]. By integrating multiple metabolic parameters into a 
single index, TyHGB can serve as an efficient marker for 
NAFLD risk assessment that accounts for the intercon­
nected nature of these metabolic factors.
The superior predictive ability of TyHGB for NAFLD is 
supported by its strong biological plausibility related to 
the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying NAFLD 
development. NAFLD demonstrates strong associations 
with metabolic dysfunction, and IR plays a central role in 
its pathogenesis. The TyG index, a component of TyHGB, 
is a well-established surrogate marker for IR, reflect­
ing impaired glucose metabolism, which contributes to 
hepatic steatosis through enhanced newly synthesized 
fat production and impaired suppression of lipolysis 
[34]. The TyHGB includes the TG and HDL-C levels, 
both of which are critical indicators of lipid metabolism 
that directly influence hepatic fat accumulation [18, 39]. 
Elevated TG levels reflect increased substrate availability 
for hepatic fat deposition, whereas reduced HDL-C lev­
els signify impaired reverse cholesterol transport, which 
normally helps remove excess cholesterol from periph­
eral tissues, including the liver. By incorporating both 
TG and HDL-C levels as a ratio, TyHGB provides a more 
complete assessment of dyslipidemia than TyG alone, 
which only accounts for TG. Obesity, which is quanti­
fied by BMI in the TyHGB formula, is a significant risk 
factor for IR and NAFLD [40]. Excess adipose tissue, 
particularly visceral fat, contributes to the pathogenesis 
of NAFLD through multiple mechanisms: (1) increased 
release of free fatty acids, which are taken up by the 
liver and contribute to hepatic steatosis; (2) production 
of pro-inflammatory adipokines that promote hepatic 
inflammation and fibrosis; and (3) induction of IR, which 
further exacerbates hepatic steatosis through dysregu­
lated glucose and lipid metabolism. The inclusion of BMI 
in TyHGB accounted for the contribution of overall adi­
posity to NAFLD risk, thereby addressing a major limita­
tion of the TyG index.
The distinct nonlinear patterns between the cohorts 
reflected population-specific metabolic thresholds. The 
J-shaped curve in the Chinese cohort, with a minimal 
risk below a TyHGB value of 7.5, indicates preserved 
metabolic flexibility at lower values: intact mitochondrial 
function, appropriate insulin signaling, and functional 
adipose tissue maintaining hepatic lipid homeosta­
sis. Once this threshold is exceeded, these compensa­
tory mechanisms become overwhelmed, leading to an 
exponential increase in the risk of NAFLD. This result 
agrees with studies demonstrating that East Asian pop­
ulations maintain metabolic health at lower BMI levels, 
but metabolic health deteriorates rapidly beyond spe­
cific thresholds [41]. The NHANES cohort’s immediate 
risk elevation at low TyHGB values indicates preexisting 
metabolic inflexibility, likely due to chronic overnutri­
tion and the dysfunctional adipose tissue characteristics 
in Western populations. The subsequent risk plateau may 
represent hepatic adaptation through the formation of 
less-lipotoxic large lipid droplets, rather than dispersed

lipid accumulation [42]. These patterns suggest that East 
Asian populations may benefit from early interventions 
targeting a TyHGB threshold of 7.5, whereas Western 
populations require aggressive intervention even at lower 
TyHGB values. This population-specific risk stratification 
can guide personalized NAFLD prevention strategies.
Notable differences in the performance of TyHGB were 
observed between the Chinese hospital and NHANES 
cohorts, with higher AUC values in the Chinese popu­
lation (0.8410 vs. 0.6492). Several factors may have 
contributed to this discrepancy. The greatest variation 
between study populations was observed in the extent of 
the TyHGB-NAFLD relationship. In the Chinese cohort, 
the odds ratio for NAFLD, when comparing the highest 
and lowest TyHGB quartiles, was substantially higher 
than that in the NHANES cohort. Thus, the relation­
ship between metabolic parameters and NAFLD risk 
may vary across populations, potentially owing to dif­
ferences in genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, 
or interactions between these elements [43]. Differences 
in baseline characteristics between the cohorts may par­
tially explain the observed disparities in performance. 
The Chinese cohort exhibited a more homogeneous 
metabolic profile, potentially allowing for clearer differ­
entiation between metabolic health states. In contrast, 
the NHANES cohort displayed greater heterogeneity in 
metabolic parameters, including a wider range of BMI 
values (particularly in the higher quartiles), which might 
have attenuated the discriminative capacity of TyHGB. 
Additionally, the NHANES cohort presented with greater 
comorbidity burden, particularly diabetes and hyperten­
sion, throughout all TyHGB quartiles, potentially con­
founding the relationship between TyHGB and NAFLD. 
The diagnostic criteria and methodologies for NAFLD 
assessment may also have contributed to the observed 
differences. Moreover, population-based differences 
in body composition and metabolic risk patterns likely 
account for the varying effectiveness of TyHGB. Asian 
populations typically exhibit metabolic dysfunction at 
lower BMI thresholds in comparison with Western popu­
lations, a phenomenon sometimes termed “metabolically 
obese normal weight” [44, 45]. This may explain why 
TyHGB, which incorporates BMI, demonstrated stronger 
associations with NAFLD in the Chinese cohort despite 
the lower average BMI values. Genetic factors influenc­
ing lipid metabolism, insulin sensitivity, and hepatic fat 
accumulation may further contribute to ethnic varia­
tions in the relationship between metabolic indices and 
NAFLD [46, 47]. Lifestyle and dietary factors that dif­
fer substantially between populations may influence the 
association between metabolic variables and NAFLD. 
Differences in dietary composition, physical activity pat­
terns, and alcohol consumption between Chinese and 
American populations can influence both the prevalence 
of metabolic disturbances and their influence on hepatic 
steatosis [48, 49]. These factors may not have been fully 
captured by TyHGB or adequately controlled for in the 
analysis, potentially contributing to performance dif­
ferences. Despite these differences, TyHGB consistently 
outperformed TyG in both populations, suggesting that 
the fundamental approach of incorporating multiple 
metabolic parameters provides improved NAFLD risk 
assessment across diverse demographic groups, even 
if the magnitude of benefit varies. The superior perfor­
mance of TyHGB in lean individuals may reflect its ability 
to capture the lipodystrophy-like phenotype [50], which 
is characterized by impaired adipose tissue expandability 
and ectopic fat deposition despite normal BMI. The com­
ponents of TyHGB, particularly the TG/HDL-C ratio, 
align with the atherogenic dyslipidemia pattern typical of 
this phenotype, potentially explaining why TyHGB shows 
stronger associations in BMI-restricted populations.
The superior discriminative ability of TyHGB in com­
parison with TyG suggests that healthcare providers 
may benefit from transitioning to this more comprehen­
sive index for NAFLD risk assessment. The components 
required for the TyHGB calculation (triglycerides, HDL-
C, FBG, and BMI) are routinely measured in standard 
clinical evaluations and do not require specialized equip­
ment or expensive assays, making them practical options 
for various healthcare settings, including resource-
limited environments. Prompt recognition of high-risk 
NAFLD individuals through TyHGB assessment may 
enable proactive preventive measure implementation 
before the occurrence of significant liver damage occurs. 
By detecting individuals at elevated risk who could ben­
efit from intensified lifestyle approaches or enhanced 
monitoring, TyHGB could facilitate a more efficient allo­
cation of healthcare resources and potentially decrease 
NAFLD-associated complication burden.
Beyond NAFLD prediction, TyHGB may also have 
broader applications in cardiometabolic risk stratifica­
tion. As noted by Stefan et al. [51], while novel metabolic 
phenotyping approaches may not universally outperform 
established risk models, they show promise for specific 
populations. The strong performance of TyHGB in lean 
individuals suggests that it could help identify those with 
metabolically unhealthy normal weight, a group with 
a disproportionately high cardiometabolic risk despite 
a normal BMI. The comprehensive nature of TyHGB, 
which incorporates lipid ratios, glucose metabolism, and 
adiposity, captures multiple dimensions of metabolic dys­
function that collectively drive CVD and diabetes risks. 
Future longitudinal studies should evaluate whether 
TyHGB can predict incident cardiovascular events and 
diabetes and potentially act as a simple, unified tool for 
metabolic risk assessment that can guide both NAFLD

screening and broader cardiometabolic risk stratification 
in clinical practice.
Study strengths and limitations
The study conclusions are supported by several strong 
design elements: the large Chinese cohort provided 
substantial statistical power for detecting meaning­
ful associations; validation across two ethnically diverse 
populations enhanced the generalizability of our conclu­
sions; our comprehensive statistical approach, including 
RCS, ROC curves, and NRI/IDI calculations, enabled 
a thorough assessment of TyHGB’s performance; and 
adjustment for potential confounders minimized the 
risk of spurious associations. Our sensitivity analysis 
also provided crucial insights into the performance of 
TyHGB under standardized conditions. When iden­
tical exclusion criteria were applied to the NHANES 
cohort, creating a population comparable to the Chinese 
cohort, TyHGB still demonstrated meaningful improve­
ment over the baseline model (ΔAUC = 0.027, P = 0.062), 
with significant improvements in both NRI (0.3168, 
P < 0.001) and IDI (0.0245, P = 0.00732). These improve­
ments were more substantial than those achieved by 
TyG (ΔAUC = 0.025, P = 0.172). However, several key 
limitations of this research deserve attention. The cross-
sectional design of both cohorts prevented the establish­
ment of temporal relationships and causal inferences. 
Selection bias may have influenced our findings, par­
ticularly in this hospital-based Chinese cohort study. 
The unavailability of blood pressure measurements and 
clinical diagnostic information in the publicly available 
Chinese cohort dataset prevented a direct comparison 
of the prevalence of comorbidities between the Chinese 
and NHANES populations, and may partially explain the 
performance differences observed between cohorts. The 
utilization of ultrasound imaging rather than hepatic 
biopsy for NAFLD identification could result in preva­
lence underestimation, and technical differences between 
cohorts may influence diagnostic consistency. The Chi­
nese cohort data obtained from a publicly available data­
base had preexisting exclusions for BMI > 25 kg/m² and 
LDL-c levels > 3.12 mmol/L. Although the analysis of 
participants outside these ranges was not possible in the 
Chinese cohort, validation in the unrestricted NHANES 
cohort, which included participants with a wide range of 
BMI and LDL-c values, demonstrated that TyHGB main­
tained superior predictive performance across diverse 
populations. Furthermore, the retrospective nature 
of the analysis may have introduced information bias. 
Despite extensive adjustments, unmeasured factors such 
as dietary habits, exercise patterns, and genetic suscepti­
bility could have confounded the observed associations. 
Finally, although strong associations between TyHGB 
and NAFLD were established in this study, interventional 
studies are required to determine whether targeting 
TyHGB components can effectively reduce the risk of 
NAFLD or improve liver outcomes. Future studies should 
validate TyHGB in individuals with BMI > 25  kg/m² to 
explore whether differential utility exists across adiposity 
phenotypes.
Clinical implementation
On the basis of these findings, we propose practical 
TyHGB thresholds for clinical decision-making d. For 
East Asian populations, TyHGB < 7.5 indicates low risk 
(annual monitoring), 7.5-9.0 suggests intermediate risk 
(biannual assessment with structured lifestyle inter­
ventions), and > 9.0 warrants high-risk management 
(quarterly monitoring, hepatic imaging, and consider­
ation for pharmacotherapy). Western populations, given 
their heightened metabolic susceptibility, require lower 
thresholds: low risk, < 6.0; intermediate risk, 6.0–8.0; 
and high risk, > 8.0. Implementation can be facilitated 
through automated calculation of electronic health 
records using routine laboratory values (TG, HDL-C, and 
FBG levels and BMI), with alert systems triggered when 
thresholds are exceeded. This risk-stratified approach 
enables efficient resource allocation, targeting intensive 
interventions for high-risk individuals while avoiding the 
overmedicalization of low-risk populations. The simplic­
ity of the TyHGB calculation, which requires only stan­
dard metabolic panel components, makes it immediately 
implementable in primary care settings without addi­
tional costs. Healthcare systems can integrate TyHGB 
into existing cardiovascular risk assessment protocols 
to create comprehensive metabolic evaluation path­
ways. Prospective studies should validate these proposed 
thresholds and evaluate whether TyHGB-guided inter­
ventions can improve clinical outcomes in comparison 
with standard care.
Conclusions
This study demonstrated that TyHGB, a novel meta­
bolic index incorporating triglyceride, HDL cholesterol, 
and FBG levels as well as BMI, exhibited superior per­
formance in predicting NAFLD in comparison with the 
established TyG index across two diverse populations. 
The nonlinear relationship between TyHGB values and 
NAFLD risk revealed population-specific metabolic 
thresholds that can guide targeted screening strategies. 
Given that TyHGB only requires routinely measured 
clinical parameters, it represents a practical tool for 
early NAFLD risk stratification in primary care settings. 
Beyond NAFLD prediction, the comprehensive meta­
bolic assessment provided by TyHGB may prove valuable 
for broader cardiometabolic risk evaluation, particularly 
in lean individuals where traditional approaches may be 
inadequate. Future prospective studies should validate

Abstract: Background As non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) becomes increasingly common and affects population health, simple and effective screening tools for NAFLD are essential. The triglyceride high-density cholesterol-glucose body index (TyHGB), a novel metabolic index, has shown promise for predicting metabolic disorders. The objective of this research was to assess TyHGB’s predictive capability for NAFLD across two distinct cohorts. Methods This retrospective study utilized data obtained from two independent cohorts: a Chinese hospital cohort (n = 181,241) and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cohort (n = 3,286). TyHGB was computed according to the following equation: triglyceride level/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol level + 0.7 × fasting blood glucose level (mmol/L) + 0.1 × body mass index (kg/m²). NAFLD was diagnosed using ultrasonography. The TyHGB-NAFLD association was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression analysis, restricted cubic spline methodology, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. To establish the added predictive capacity of TyHGB over the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) were determined. Results In both cohorts, participants with higher TyHGB values demonstrated a significantly higher prevalence of NAFLD. After full adjustment for potential confounders, the odds ratios for NAFLD on comparing the highest versus lowest quartiles of TyHGB were 12.22 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.73–13.93) in the Chinese cohort and 3.17 (95% CI: 2.25–4.46) in the NHANES cohort. Restricted cubic spline modeling demonstrated significant nonlinear associations between TyHGB values and NAFLD risk in both populations (P for nonlinearity < 0.001). TyHGB demonstrated superior discriminative ability for NAFLD in comparison with the TyG index, with area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.8410 versus 0.7995 in the Chinese cohort and 0.6492 versus 0.5952 in the NHANES cohort (both P < 0.001). Adding TyHGB to the baseline prediction models significantly improved risk discrimination, with greater improvements than those achieved by adding TyG (NRI: 0.0183, 95% CI: 0.015–0.0217; IDI: 0.0067, 95% CI: 0.0057– 0.0076; both P < 0.001).
